title: Computational Thinking Skills
overview: Topic 9.1 is about two thinking skills used before any code is written. Abstraction strips a problem down to the details that actually affect the result, giving a simpler model to design against. Decomposition splits the problem into sub-problems small enough to solve one at a time, and each sub-problem becomes a program module: a procedure or a function. Paper 2 questions give a short scenario and expect you to apply both skills to it: name the details you would keep and drop, and name the modules you would write and what each one does.
syllabusPoints: Show an understanding of abstraction, including the need for and benefits of using abstraction, and describe the purpose of abstraction.
Produce an abstract model of a system by only including essential details.
Describe and use decomposition: break down problems into sub-problems leading to the concept of a program module (procedure / function).

definitions.definition: A logical way of analysing a problem and building a solution that a person can follow and a computer can carry out; it draws on abstraction, decomposition, data modelling, pattern recognition and algorithm design.
Filtering out the details of a problem that do not affect the solution, so that attention stays on the information that does.
A simplified representation of a real system that keeps only the essential data and behaviour needed for the task, such as a route map that shows stations and connections but not streets.
Breaking a problem into smaller sub-problems, each of which can be understood, solved and tested separately; the sub-problems lead to program modules.
A named, self-contained block of steps that carries out one sub-task and can be called from elsewhere in the program; in 9618 pseudocode a module is a procedure or a function.
A module given an identifier that performs a sub-task when it is called with a CALL statement; it does not itself return a value to an expression.
A module given an identifier that returns a single value of a stated data type; a function call is written inside an expression, for example Total ← Total + VAT(Price).
Spotting that a problem, or part of one, matches a problem already solved, so a known method or standard algorithm can be reused.
Designing a solution by starting from the whole problem and repeatedly splitting each part into smaller parts until every part is simple enough to program.

sections.title: What computational thinking is
content: Computational thinking is the set of habits a programmer uses to turn a vague real-world problem into something a computer can solve. The emphasis is on analysis before code: working out what the problem really is, what data matters, and what steps will produce the answer. The coursebook groups the skills into strands: abstraction, decomposition, data modelling, pattern recognition and algorithm design.

The 9618 AS syllabus examines two of these directly, abstraction and decomposition, and uses the others as supporting ideas. Algorithm design itself is developed in 9.2, where the steps are written as structured English, flowcharts and pseudocode.
bullets: Abstraction answers 'what do I need to know?'; decomposition answers 'what are the separate jobs?'.
Both are applied before writing pseudocode, which is why exam questions on them usually come with an unfamiliar scenario.
The skills feed into each other: an abstract model shows which data exists, and decomposition decides which module handles which part of it.

sections.title: Abstraction and its purpose
content: Abstraction means deliberately leaving out detail that has no effect on the result you need. A real situation always contains far more information than a program could or should hold. The purpose of abstraction is to reduce that situation to a model containing only what the solution depends on, so the designer can concentrate on the parts that matter.

A familiar example is a metro or bus network map. The real routes curve through streets, tunnels and hills, yet a passenger planning a journey only needs to know which stops exist, which lines join them and the order of the stops. The map keeps exactly that and drops distances, geography and street names. It is less 'accurate' than an aerial photograph, but far more useful for the task.

Abstraction also appears inside programming itself. An algorithm is an abstraction of a process: it states the inputs, steps and outputs and ignores how the hardware carries them out. Calling a module such as CALL PrintReceipt hides the detail of how the receipt is laid out, so the caller only needs to know what the module does.
bullets: The test for a detail is: would changing it change the output? If not, it can be abstracted away.
What counts as essential depends on the task. A car's colour is irrelevant to a parking charge but essential to a paint shop's stock system.
A game or simulator uses abstraction too: it keeps what the player must see and control and hides the complex rules running underneath.

sections.title: The need for abstraction and its benefits
content: Abstraction is needed because a computer system cannot model the whole of reality, and trying to include everything makes a design unmanageable. Every extra data item has to be input, validated, stored and tested. Removing what the problem does not need keeps the program focused on its actual requirements.

The benefits appear throughout development. Design is quicker because there is less to think about. The program is smaller, so it takes less time to write and test and uses less memory and storage. The customer gets a system that does what was asked without clutter, and the solution is easier for other programmers to read and maintain later.
bullets: Less data to collect and store: fewer inputs, smaller files, less validation code.
Simpler, shorter programs that are faster to develop, test and debug.
Reduced complexity lets the designer see the core problem and spot when it matches a known solution.
Hiding the inner detail of a module means it can be reused without the user needing to understand how it works.
Risk to manage: removing a detail that turns out to matter gives a model that produces wrong results, so each omission must be justified.

sections.title: Producing an abstract model of a system
content: To produce an abstract model, start from the scenario, list every piece of information it mentions, then keep only the items the required outputs depend on. What remains becomes the data your program will hold (later, the fields of a record or the columns of a table) plus the operations the system must carry out on that data.

Worked scenario: a school library wants a system that records loans and reminds students when a book is overdue. The scenario describes the building, the shelves, each book's cover, page count and price, and each student's name, form, photo and date of birth. The model needs far less than that.
bullets: State each item you keep and say which output or operation needs it.
State each item you drop and give the reason it does not affect the outputs.
An abstract model includes behaviour as well as data: here, 'lend', 'return' and 'check overdue'.

examples.label: Abstract model for a library loans system
examples.content:
Required outputs: record a loan, record a return, list overdue loans with the student to remind.

Kept (essential)            | Why it is needed
BookID                      | identifies which copy is on loan
Title                       | shown on the reminder so the student knows which book
StudentID                   | links the loan to one borrower
StudentName, TutorGroup     | needed to deliver the reminder
DateBorrowed, DateDue       | DateDue decides whether a loan is overdue
DateReturned (empty if out) | shows whether the book is still on loan

Dropped (not essential)     | Why it can go
Cover colour, page count    | no output depends on them
Shelf layout of the library | not needed to lend or remind
Student photo, date of birth| the reminder does not use them
Price of the book           | not needed unless the school charges for lost books

Operations in the model: LendBook, ReturnBook, ListOverdue.
If the requirement later adds charging for lost books, Price moves into the 'kept' list: essential always means essential for the stated task.

sections.title: Decomposition
content: Decomposition breaks a large problem into sub-problems. Each sub-problem is smaller, so it is easier to understand, to solve and to test on its own. If a sub-problem is still too large, it is decomposed again, giving a hierarchy that goes from the whole problem at the top down to small tasks at the bottom. Working in this direction is called top-down design.

Decomposition helps a team as well as an individual. Separate sub-problems can be given to different programmers, finished in parallel and tested independently before being put together. It also makes errors easier to find, because a fault can be traced to one sub-problem rather than hunted for across the whole program, and it shows up tasks that repeat so they can be written once and reused.
bullets: Stop decomposing when each task is small enough to write as one short module.
Good sub-problems have one clear job and a clear set of inputs and outputs.
Testing each part alone is not enough: the parts must also be tested together to check they pass data correctly.

examples.label: Decomposing a revision quiz program
examples.content:
Quiz program
|-- 1 Set up the quiz
|     |-- 1.1 Read the questions and answers from a file
|     |-- 1.2 Ask the player for their name
|-- 2 Run the quiz (repeat for each question)
|     |-- 2.1 Display the question
|     |-- 2.2 Input the player's answer
|     |-- 2.3 Check whether the answer is correct
|     |-- 2.4 Update the score
|-- 3 Finish
      |-- 3.1 Output the final score
      |-- 3.2 Save the score if it is a new high score

Each bottom-level box is small enough to become one module, e.g. 2.3 becomes
FUNCTION IsCorrect(Given : STRING, Expected : STRING) RETURNS BOOLEAN

sections.title: Pattern recognition, data modelling and algorithm design
content: The other strands of computational thinking support abstraction and decomposition. Pattern recognition notices that a sub-problem has the same shape as one already solved. Finding the highest score, the most expensive product and the hottest day are all 'keep the largest value seen so far'. Recognising that lets you reuse a tested method, or a standard algorithm such as a linear search or bubble sort.

Data modelling decides how the data kept by abstraction will be organised: records, arrays, files or abstract data types such as stacks and queues (topic 10). Algorithm design turns each sub-problem into a precise sequence of steps (topic 9.2).
bullets: Patterns only become visible after abstraction has removed the scenario-specific detail.
Reusing a known pattern saves design and testing time.
Data modelling links 9.1 to records and abstract data types in 10.1 and 10.4.

sections.title: From sub-problems to program modules
content: When a problem has been decomposed, each sub-task can be written as a module: a named group of steps that is written once and called whenever that sub-task is needed. In 9618 pseudocode there are two kinds. A procedure performs a task and is run with a CALL statement. A function performs a task and returns one value, so its call is placed inside an expression, and its header states the data type of the value it returns.

The main program then reads like the top level of the decomposition: a short list of calls. Modules should be self-contained. They receive the data they need through parameters and use local variables for their own working, rather than relying on global variables. This makes each module independent, easy to test alone and reusable in other programs.
bullets: Use a function when the sub-task produces one value to be used in a calculation or condition; use a procedure otherwise.
Module identifiers follow the same naming rules as variable identifiers.
A module can call other modules, mirroring lower levels of the decomposition.
Parameters and local variables are covered in detail in 11.3.

examples.label: A decomposed program: a function, a procedure and a short main program
examples.content:
FUNCTION ToFahrenheit(Celsius : REAL) RETURNS REAL
   RETURN Celsius * 9 / 5 + 32
ENDFUNCTION

PROCEDURE ShowConversion(Celsius : REAL)
   OUTPUT Celsius, " C = ", ToFahrenheit(Celsius), " F"
ENDPROCEDURE

// main program
DECLARE Reading : REAL
DECLARE Count : INTEGER
FOR Count ← 1 TO 3
   INPUT Reading
   CALL ShowConversion(Reading)
NEXT Count

examples.label: Trace table for the module example (inputs 0, 100, -40)
examples.content:
Count | Reading | ToFahrenheit(Reading)  | OUTPUT
1     | 0       | 0 * 9 / 5 + 32 = 32    | 0 C = 32 F
2     | 100     | 900 / 5 + 32 = 212     | 100 C = 212 F
3     | -40     | -360 / 5 + 32 = -40    | -40 C = -40 F

The loop ends after Count = 3. The main program never repeats the formula: it is written once in the function and reached through the procedure.

A simplified abstract model of the system

diagram.title: From scenario to program modules
nodes: Read the scenario and its required outputs
Abstraction: keep only the details the outputs depend on
Abstract model: essential data and operations
Decomposition: split the problem into sub-problems
Refine each sub-problem until it is one small task
Write each task as a procedure or function
Main program calls the modules in order

analysisChains.title: Abstracting a car park charging system
steps: The scenario lists each car's registration, colour, make, driver, entry time and exit time
The required output is the charge, which depends only on the length of stay
Colour, make and driver do not change the charge, so they are left out of the model
Registration is kept only if a receipt must identify the car; entry and exit times are essential
analysisChains.evaluation: The model is judged against the stated outputs: a detail is kept only if some output depends on it, which is why the same data item can be essential in one system and irrelevant in another.

analysisChains.title: Decomposing a school library system into modules
steps: 'Run the library' is too large to design or test as one algorithm
It splits into lending, returning, searching the catalogue and listing overdue loans
Listing overdue loans splits again into reading each loan, comparing DateDue with today and outputting a reminder
Each bottom-level task becomes a module, e.g. FUNCTION IsOverdue(DateDue : DATE) RETURNS BOOLEAN
analysisChains.evaluation: Decomposition gives modules that can be written and tested separately and shared across a team, but the finished modules still need testing together because faults often sit in the data passed between them.

analysisChains.title: Why a route map is a good abstraction
steps: A traveller needs to know which stops exist and which lines connect them
Real track shapes, distances and street layout do not change which route to take
The map drops them and draws lines straight with evenly spaced stops
The simpler picture makes route planning faster and less error-prone
analysisChains.evaluation: The map is less realistic but more useful, which is the point of abstraction: the model is judged by how well it serves its purpose, not by how much detail it holds.

examTips: In an 'apply abstraction' question, name specific items from the scenario you would keep and drop, with a reason tied to the required output; a general definition alone earns little.
For benefits of abstraction, give concrete effects: less data to input and store, smaller programs, faster development and testing, a solution focused on the customer's actual needs.
When asked to decompose, give sub-problems with one clear job each, and say which would be procedures and which would be functions.
A function returns a single value and is called inside an expression; a procedure is called with CALL. Examiners often reward this distinction.
Link decomposition to modules explicitly: the syllabus wording is 'leading to the concept of a program module'.
commonMistakes: Defining abstraction as 'hiding complexity' without saying what is removed or why it is not needed.
Dropping a detail that an output depends on, such as removing entry time from a parking-charge model.
Confusing abstraction (removing detail) with decomposition (splitting into parts).
Listing sub-problems that are just the whole problem reworded, or so large they still cannot be written as one module.
Writing a function without a RETURNS data type or calling a procedure inside an expression.
Letting modules share global variables instead of passing data as parameters, which stops them being reused.

quickRecall.question: What is the purpose of abstraction?
quickRecall.answer: To remove details that do not affect the solution so the designer can concentrate on the essential information, giving a simpler model of the problem.

quickRecall.question: Give three benefits of using abstraction.
quickRecall.answer: Less data to input and store; smaller, simpler programs that are quicker to write and test; a solution focused on what the customer actually needs.

quickRecall.question: How do you decide whether a detail belongs in an abstract model?
quickRecall.answer: Keep it only if a required output or operation of the system depends on it.

quickRecall.question: What is decomposition?
quickRecall.answer: Breaking a problem into smaller sub-problems that can be solved and tested separately.

quickRecall.question: What does decomposition lead to in a program?
quickRecall.answer: Program modules: each sub-problem becomes a procedure or a function.

quickRecall.question: State the difference between a procedure and a function.
quickRecall.answer: A procedure is called with CALL to perform a task; a function returns one value of a stated type and is called inside an expression.

quickRecall.question: Why should modules use parameters and local variables?
quickRecall.answer: So each module is self-contained, can be tested on its own and can be reused in other programs.
